title: Zuckerberg Apologizes to India Over CSAM on Meta Platforms and Modi Post Restriction
excerpt: The Meta CEO's apology came as the Indian government pressed the company over child sexual abuse ads on Instagram, deepfake content, and the brief blocking of a post by Prime Minister Modi.
body:
• Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg apologized to the Indian government over child sexual abuse material on Meta platforms, deepfake content, and other operational lapses, according to Indian media reports
  • Separately, Meta's Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan apologized for briefly restricting a post by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in July, calling it an "operational error"
  • India's IT ministry had ordered Meta in July to remove Instagram ads promoting CSAM after a BBC investigation uncovered paid advertisements for abuse material on the platform
  • Police in Hyderabad registered a case against Meta India head Arun Srinivas over Facebook videos allegedly depicting Modi in an abusive manner

The Apology

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg apologized to the Indian government over child sexual abuse material on the company's platforms, deepfake content, and operational errors, Indian financial publication Moneycontrol and local TV channels reported on Wednesday.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=T7KCfhgr_4s

The apology was conveyed during a meeting between Meta executives and Indian government officials, according to the reports. Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

Separately, Meta's Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan issued a public apology for the brief restriction of a post by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in July.

"I apologised to the minister on behalf of Meta for the error restricting PM Modi's post."

— Joel Kaplan, Meta Chief Global Affairs Officer

The Modi Post Incident

Last month, India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology summoned Meta executives after Facebook briefly restricted a video message by Modi — his first public address on the massive student protests that forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. The post, which has more than 404 million views on Instagram, was blocked temporarily on Facebook.

Meta said the post had been restricted inadvertently because of an operational error. S. Krishnan, secretary at the IT ministry, said at the time that the government had asked Meta "to come in at the highest level and explain what is happening."

The incident came during a period of heightened tension between Modi's government and the tech company. Modi has faced what Reuters described as "the biggest wave of youth-led protests India has seen in more than a decade," sparked by leaked papers in national examinations.

CSAM on Instagram

The Indian government's pressure on Meta over child sexual abuse material followed a BBC World Service investigation published on July 4 that found paid advertisements on Instagram promoting CSAM. Some ads used terms such as "rape video" and "child video," directing users to Telegram channels where the material was allegedly being sold for as little as 99 rupees (approximately $1.20).

India's IT ministry ordered Meta to remove the ads and content, and demanded an explanation within seven days on how such advertisements had appeared on the platform. Meta said at the time that it had a "zero-tolerance policy" on CSAM and was "continuing to strengthen its detection systems."

Legal Pressure Mounting

The regulatory pressure extends beyond the IT ministry. Police in the southern Indian city of Hyderabad registered a case against Meta India head Arun Srinivas over videos posted on Facebook that allegedly depicted Modi in an "abusive manner," Reuters reported last week. The videos spread during the protest movement.

India is Facebook's largest market by users. The series of incidents — the Modi post blocking, the CSAM advertising, and the deepfake content — represents a significant escalation in tensions between Meta and the Indian government, which has increasingly asserted authority over social media content within its borders.

Zuckerberg's direct apology marks a rare instance of the Meta CEO personally addressing a foreign government's content-related complaints. The company has faced similar scrutiny from regulators in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Australia, but India's combination of market scale and regulatory assertiveness gives it particular leverage.
nri_angle: India is Meta's largest market by users, and the regulatory showdown affects how billions of Indian users experience Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.
